item.title: AI doesn’t care about your job title
item.description: One person works across a design file, a product roadmap, and a code editor at a single desk, with their badge face down beside the keyboard. AI assisted, steampunk style.Exposure to artificial intelligence runs through the tasks you do each week, not the role on your badge. Here’s how to measure yours and lower the risk.My mom doesn’t understand my job, and it isn’t her fault. The closest I’ve ever come to explaining it is “I design how it works,” which is true and tells her almost nothing about my day.It also works best when I’m wearing a black turtleneck and holding an iPhone, channeling my inner Steve Jobs.That’s the curse of knowledge, and I’ve never directly defined my role in many of the places I’ve worked. Over decades I’ve managed design, product management, and engineering, and more than once I started without a job description. It wasn’t about my job title, it was about judgement applied through my experience building software.Artificial intelligence doesn’t care about your job title or mine. It’s probabilistically predicting an outcome without looking at your LinkedIn.In GPTs are GPTs, published in 2023, researchers from OpenAI and the University of Pennsylvania scored occupations task by task. They estimated that 80% of U.S. workers could see at least a tenth of their tasks affected, and about 19% could see at least half.Those averages hide what matters for one person. Your exposure depends on how much of your week can be specified briefly and checked quickly, and seniority protects you only when it changes that mix.Her work.For her work, she’s not exposed even though she’s in the models. From Claude:The main trace of Jean Neeman in the art world is a single, well-documented piece: a teapot titled “Tea on the Go,” made in 1994 by Jean Neeman (American, b. 1948) from silver, copper, brass, and cocobolo wood, measuring about 8.4 x 7.75 x 4.5 inches. That puts her work alongside some serious company.She doesn’t have to measure her risk because she’s an artist. I measure mine all the time so I can add value that AI can’t add, and that’s judgement.The five steps below show how to measure yours, each with a prompt to run in Claude.List Your Actual TasksStart with a week, not a job description.List everything you spent more than half an hour on: the usability readout, the stakeholder review, the status update nobody read. Note the hours, how often each task repeats, and who reviews the result.Also leave room for the white space between tasks.Unblocking a teammate, the quick answer that saves someone a day, the thinking before a hard review: none of it shows up in a job description or on a calendar. It also goes unseen when people judge what you do, whether that’s a manager at review time or a researcher scoring tasks for exposure.It’s often where you absorb complexity that, as Tesler’s Law puts it, can be moved but never removed.Write it down anyway.For a checklist, O*NET OnLine, the Labor Department’s occupational database, lists 31 tasks for Web and Digital Interface Designers. In Putting Tasks to the Test: Human Capital, Job Tasks and Wages, a 2009 paper, economists David Autor and Michael Handel found that tasks vary substantially within occupations, enough to predict wage gaps among people who hold the same job.ATMs didn’t kill the teller, iPhones did.In Toil and Technology, written for the International Monetary Fund in 2015, economist James Bessen showed how automated teller machines took over dispensing cash and taking deposits. The tellers needed to run an average urban branch fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004, but banks opened 43% more urban branches, so the jobs held.The title stayed the same while the job underneath it was rebuilt.My own title changed in March, from director to senior principal designer. Neither title would tell you which of my tasks a model can do, but my calendar would.Try It in ClaudeRun these prompts in one Claude conversation. The first one drafts your week from your role, so you correct a list instead of writing one, and you can check its tasks against O*NET OnLine.To map my exposure to artificial intelligence, don’t read my calendar or connected accounts, or ask me to describe my week. If you don’t know my title, ask once. Name the O*NET occupation you matched, and say if you’re recalling its tasks from memory. Draft 15 to 20 tasks from it, plus the undocumented work between them, for a normal week. Give hours, frequency, and reviewer for each, marked as guesses. Then have me correct it, including whether I manage anyone.Score Each Task’s ExposureDifficulty is a poor guide to exposure. In a 2023 experiment for Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, a team led by Fabrizio Dell’Acqua gave 758 Boston Consulting Group consultants realistic work.With the model, they did far better on 18 tasks inside its abilities but were 19 percentage points less likely to get the right answer on one task outside them. Coauthor Ethan Mollick calls this the jagged frontier in Centaurs and Cyborgs on the Jagged Frontier: tasks that look equally hard can sit on opposite sides of an invisible wall.Score each task with two questions instead. I call it the spec-and-check test.Specify the result. Ask whether you could describe a finished version in two sentences that someone else could follow.Check the output. Ask whether someone could confirm it’s right in less time than it took to make.A task that’s quick to specify and quick to check is exposed, whatever your title says.Twenty variations of an empty state pass both questions. Deciding which of three problems to fund this quarter fails both, and for now that decision stays yours.Then weight the list by hours, because the Pareto Principle usually holds and a few tasks fill most of the week. A task that passes both and fills two days a week is where your risk sits.When leadership reviews a pie chart of where a team’s hours go, you don’t want to be on the wrong side of it.Passing the test means a model could do the task, not that one already does. In Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence, from its own March 2026 usage data, Anthropic found Claude covering about 33% of computer and math tasks, against 94% rated feasible in GPTs are GPTs.So the prompt below has Claude try one.Try It in ClaudePaste this after the task table. It ends with Claude attempting your most exposed task, so you judge real output instead of a forecast.Score each task in my table: could a finished version be described in two sentences, and checked faster than it took to make? Answer yes, partly, or no for each. Then say honestly if you could do each task today, fully, partly, or not yet, and why. Mark tasks with two yeses as exposed, sort by hours, and tell me what share of my week is exposed. Offer to try my top exposed task so I can judge it.Check Your Career StageIn the August 2026 revision of Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab found no economy-wide job displacement in payroll data. Employment for workers ages 22 to 25 in exposed occupations, though, sits 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, mostly because companies are hiring fewer young people.Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial IntelligenceExperienced workers show no comparable gap, and the authors call these early indicators, not proof of cause.Entry-level work is often the most specified on a team, handed down with clear instructions and reviewed by someone senior, which is where a model does best. Experience protects through judgment and context that rarely fit in a two-sentence spec.A senior title over a week of status decks is junior exposure with a bigger paycheck.If you’re early in your career, ask to own one small decision from start to finish. If you’re senior, hand your juniors judgment calls along with tasks.Management will also change because there will be smaller teams.Melvin Conway observed in 1968 that organizations build systems that copy their communication structures, which I cover in Conway’s Law. My extension is that much of management exists to carry that communication, so a smaller team needs less of it. Four people share six possible pairs, while 10 people share 45.The flattening predates these tools. For The Manager Mass Exodus: How SMBs Are Flattening the Org Chart, Gusto studied payroll at about 8,500 small and midsize businesses. The share of their workers who manage anyone fell from just under 25% in 2019 to about 15% by late 2024. If you manage, move your hours from relaying information toward the decisions and coaching a smaller team still needs.Try It in ClaudeThis prompt compares your task list against your experience. Correct it if it gets your background wrong.Based on my title and experience, split my tasks into entry-level work (well specified and reviewed by others) and judgment work only I can do. If you don’t know my years of experience, ask once. Give the share of hours in each and, if I manage, how much goes to relaying information. Name the knowledge I bring that you could supply without my judgment. Tell me plainly if my week looks junior for my title, and suggest one decision I could own this quarter.Deepen Your Domain ExpertiseKnowing your field pays off more than knowing your tools. For Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise, published in June 2026, Anthropic studied about 400,000 Claude Code sessions.Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertisePeople made about 70% of the planning decisions — that’s human agency — and the agent made about 80% of the execution decisions.The researchers rated expertise task by task and said it differs from job title: a senior engineer asking a first question about the Rust language counts as a beginner at Rust. Expert sessions succeeded about twice as often as novice ones, and a working grasp of the domain captured most of that gain, the same early-steep curve as the Power Law of Practice.The person who understands the problem and not the model gets more out than the person who understands the model and not the problem.Knowledge on its own doesn’t protect you anymore: If what you know can be pulled from a large language model without judgment to apply it, you’re at risk.Companies don’t need you to tell them something they already know, they need the person who knows which answer fits this customer and this quarter, and the person who acts as connective tissue between people, building trust and getting decisions made rather than relaying status.If you’re neither, your expertise is a search ot an AI Assistant result.For designers, the domain is the user’s world and the business around it. Get closer to your users’ domain than your product manager is: read the regulations your customers follow, sit with support for a day, and learn how the money moves.Try It in ClaudeAnswer the way you would with a new manager, without polishing. Short, unsure answers show the gaps fastest.If you don’t know what my company sells, ask once. Tell me in one sentence who my product serves, and let me correct it. Ask me eight to 10 questions, one at a time, about their regulations, money, metrics, and workflow; “not sure” is a fine answer. Rank my knowledge gaps by how much they’d change my design decisions, suggest one way to close the top gap in 30 days, and revise the decision you suggested earlier.Rebuild Your PortfolioEmployers expect 39% of workers’ core skills to change by 2030, according to the World Economic Forum’s The Future of Jobs Report 2025. A portfolio of polished final screens puts the fastest-changing part of your job up front and hides the part that holds its value.The Future of Jobs Report 2025 — much of what employers value can’t be done by an agent.Rebuild it around decisions: the problem you chose and the ones you turned down, the tradeoff and why, and what happened after launch. Show one case where you directed a model, caught its mistake, and shipped the fix.Show the work a model couldn’t have done without you.Look sideways too.O*NET lists 10 related occupations for the same designer category, from software developers to graphic designers, and jobs overlap where their tasks do. As I wrote in We’ve Seen This Movie Before: Desktop Publishing Already Showed Us How AI Prototyping Plays Out, typesetting effectively ended as a profession while graphic design grew into web, motion, and product design. They all adjusted, and we’re seeing this move now too.Whole economies have also made this move before.The 20th Century Transformation of U.S. Agriculture and Farm PolicyThe agricultural revolution let fewer people grow more food, and the industrial revolution absorbed the workers it freed. In 1900, 41% of American workers farmed, and by 2000 fewer than 2% did, according to The 20th Century Transformation of U.S. Agriculture and Farm Policy from the USDA’s Economic Research Service.The adjustment wasn’t gentle, though.In Engels’ Pause, economic historian Robert Allen found that British wages stalled for roughly half a century in the early industrial era while output per worker kept climbing.People adjusted, but it took a generation, and the ones who fared best moved toward the new work instead of waiting for it to reach them.The good news is that employers now have software to map those overlaps, something Henry Ford never had. When Ford ended the Model T in 1927, about 60,000 workers were laid off, according to Last Day of Model T Production at Ford from HISTORY. Skills platforms such as Skills Cloud, from my employer Workday, now relate the skills across a workforce.The Future of Jobs Report 2025In the report’s workforce strategies chapter, 85% of employers plan to upskill and 51% plan to move staff into growing roles. Organizations are looking to reinvest and reinvent.Intentions aren’t programs, though, as Dan Maccarone argues in What the AI era owes you for UX Collective Editors. You own your career, not your company.It’s up to you to figure out where the hockey puck is going, the advice Wayne Gretzky got from his father, Walter, and your task list shows which way it’s moving.Try It in ClaudeRun this on your strongest case study first. Then reuse it on the rest, and keep the list of adjacent jobs it produces.Ask me for my strongest case study. Rewrite it around my decisions: the problem, the options I turned down, the tradeoff, how I used and corrected artificial intelligence tools (or that I didn’t), and the outcome. Ask for missing facts one at a time instead of inventing them. Then list four or five jobs whose tasks overlap most with mine, what I’d need to add for each, and which carry more exposure than mine, using the earlier test.ConclusionThe tellers’ story has a second chapter, and the branch boom that saved their jobs didn’t last. The Bureau of Labor Statistics outlook for Tellers projects employment falling 13% from 2025 to 2035, as mobile deposits and online banking keep customers away from the window. The first wave of automation changed what tellers did, and the second is taking away where they did it.That’s why the task list is a recurring exercise. Models improve unevenly, and a task that failed the spec-and-check test last spring can pass it next spring. Redo the list every six months and move a few more hours toward the work a model can’t finish without you.There will always need to be a human in the loop, the person who commits to what the system proposes, as my Human-in-the-Loop entry puts it. Beyond that, there has to be human agency: someone who decides rather than someone who clicks approve.My mom won’t be able to explain my job, whatever the next title is. A model won’t need the title to find my exposed work, and it can point out where it is.Run the first prompt next Monday, before the next reorganization or the next model release decides the mix for you and how you can explain it to your mom.Action itemsDraft your task list. Run the first prompt and correct the table it builds from your role, or log every task longer than 30 minutes for five days by hand, using the O*NET task list for your occupation to catch what you missed.Score each task. Mark whether a finished version can be specified in two sentences and checked faster than it was made, and treat tasks that pass both as your exposure.Trade one hour. Each week, move an hour from your most exposed task to a planning decision, a stakeholder conversation, or time with users.Rewrite one case study. Rebuild your strongest portfolio piece around the decisions you made, including any evaluation criteria you wrote and what happened after launch, and note which adjacent job its tasks would also qualify you for.AI doesn’t care about your job title was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Human attention is the new old bottleneck. We have to design for it even more.
item.description: A wide office floor where one person reads at a desk while dozens of screens around them keep filling with new work for them to address.Agents at Anthropic now log six hours for every human hour, and reading their output would eat half a week. The job is to create judgement systems for what deserves attention.On October 16, four researchers at Anthropic published How employment is changing at Anthropic, a study of how its own agents changed the work.Anthropic is one of the companies at the front of this shift, running its own work on the models it builds, so the study is an early read on where other companies are heading.And honestly, it looks like previous studies in new clothing as I have linked below, just accelerated. Read on.Agents work more than humans. Not a surprise.Here are the early results: By August 2026, agents directed by employees were logging six hours for every hour their people worked.Agent sessions spent about 80% of their time idle, waiting for a person to answer. Even for employees who don’t write code, reading everything their agents produced would take more than half the workweek.That’s the reading tax, and every team with agents will pay it.None of this is new — we have decades of research and many, many principles like Automation Bias that we can apply to solve these problems. Now it’s up to us to apply them.This productivity is changing for everyone.Underneath the numbers, the nature of work is changing yet again, and this time it’s turning everyone into a manager instead of a maker of widgets. That makes this a story about human in the loop and who keeps the agency. A person who can’t read what an agent did is still in the loop on paper, while the agent makes the calls.That puts the problem on ground designers, product managers, and researchers already work.Here are seven steps for keeping people in charge of that loop.Measure Reading TimeHerbert Simon saw this coming in 1971. In Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World, he wrote that “a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention,” with most of the cost landing on whoever receives it. He meant data banks, and the line fits agents better.Gloria Mark at UC Irvine has measured how thin it already is.Her studies from 2016 to 2020 found people stayed on one screen for 47 seconds on average. Her first study, published in 2004, found two and a half minutes, according to the University of California’s How to sharpen your attention and meet your goals in 2024.Every agent you add is a new sender in an inbox that was already overflowing with more information.Note: Hours estimated by converting output tokens to words, assuming 0.75 words per token and 250 words read per minute. What’s lost in here is that a lot of work goes unreviewed, no human in the loop.Anthropic measured the agent side the way a designer would, converting each session’s output into words read at 250 words a minute.Even non-technical groups crossed half a workweek of reading.Most days I build now, with a coding agent doing much of the work, and my limit is how much I can read and judge. So treat reading time like page load time, a budget a team sets and defends.What’s lost in here is that a lot of work goes unreviewed, no human in the loop. Four hundred and twenty four hours is a lot more than the 168 a week currently has.If one workflow’s weekly agent output, divided by 250, comes to more hours than anyone has, the workflow has a design problem.Rank Agent RequestsOne Anthropic engineer compared managing agents to babysitting. A child who needs a juice box opened and a child with a cut finger both arrive at full volume, and so do the agents.Hospitals learned what that costs.Joint Commission’s 2013 Sentinel Event Alert on medical device alarm safety estimated that 85% to 99% of alarm signals don’t require clinical intervention. Staff stop hearing them which is alarm fatigue in spades. Its database logged 80 alarm-related deaths between January 2009 and June 2012.An agent that flags everything at the same volume has trained its human to ignore it.Hospitals answered with alarm management: priorities, quiet defaults for routine readings, and a named person who responds. Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown at Xerox PARC described the goal in The Coming Age of Calm Technology in 1996, as technology that moves from the periphery of attention to the center and back.Most agent interfaces skip the periphery and drop every request in the center.Make agents justify a severity level for each request, keep the routine ones in the periphery as a digest, and bring only decisions a person must make to the center.At Anthropic, agents mostly post in channels set aside for Claude-human work, which keeps the threads where people talk readable.Design the Review StepReview is where people pay the reading tax, and it’s where a human in the loop either keeps agency or hands it over. At Anthropic, agent-written code was removed or reverted at the same rates as code the same engineers wrote by hand, though the authors caution that agent errors may be harder to spot.Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer ProductivityPerception is the bigger risk. In Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, a 2025 trial, METR found that 16 experienced developers took 19% longer with artificial intelligence tools after expecting to save 24%.If people can’t tell how long review takes, they can’t tell when they’ve stopped doing it.Andrej Karpathy made the same point in Andrej Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again), his June 2025 keynote for Y Combinator. Models generate and people verify, he said, so the loop between them should run as fast as possible, with the model kept “on the leash.”My Automation Bias entry on UX Guidelines covers what happens when that cycle slackens: people approve what the machine proposes and miss what it never flagged.A review screen should show what changed next to what existed, what the agent checked and skipped, and where each claim came from.Put the riskiest change first, and log review time per item so the team can see the tax.Write Decisions DownA manager’s decisions only count if the agents can see them. Agents reason from whatever people leave in the open. One Anthropic employee’s name stayed on a months-old document about company swag, so agents kept sending them requests for T-shirts and mugs long after the job changed hands.Shopify’s chief executive, Tobias Lütke, gave this work its popular name in June 2025. He preferred “context engineering” to prompt engineering and called it the core skill, as Simon Willison recorded in Context engineering.Anthropic’s engineers add, in Effective context engineering for AI agents, that a model’s context is a finite attention budget. Every loop runs on two budgets, the agent’s context and the person’s reading time.The cheapest way to protect a person’s attention is to write the decision down once, where every agent can find it.At Anthropic, written standing instructions for agents grew from a few hundred to 8,500 in a year. Meeting time grew 20% for the median employee and agents see none of a meeting unless someone writes it up.For design and research teams, this is familiar work. Decision logs, research repositories, and design rationale used to be documentation few people opened.Now agents read every page, which raises the bar for keeping it current and owned.Manage the AgentsAt Anthropic, a fifth of employees surveyed in April 2026 said their role had shifted from doing the work to managing Claudes, and interviewees described individual contributors making VP-level decisions. Peter Drucker saw the first version of this in The Effective Executive in 1967, writing that “every knowledge worker in a modern organization is an ‘executive’” if they’re responsible for a contribution.Agents extend that to anyone with a login, and Microsoft’s The 2025 Annual Work Trend Index: The Frontier Firm is born has a name for the role: agent boss.I call it the work about the work, and the report calls the supporting work meta-work: specifications for multi-agent runs, loops where one agent reviews another, and pipeline dashboards.It grew from 10% of employees’ interactive sessions in fall 2025 to 22% in spring 2026. Ethan Mollick argues in Management as AI superpower that this is ordinary management. What’s scarce, he writes, is “knowing what to ask for.”Every one of those homemade dashboards is a product nobody designed.Christopher Noessel argued for designing this layer in Designing Agentive Technology in 2017. Anthropic’s content team shows where it leads: the writers behind the greetings on Claude.ai taught agents to write that copy, then moved into writing prompts and evaluations.Designers and researchers already have a manager’s skills here; the job is to claim this layer before it hardens into internal scripts.Hire for JudgmentAt Anthropic, an automated review of interview scorecards found that mentions of candidates’ creative use of artificial intelligence tools roughly tripled for technical roles and quadrupled for non-technical ones between 2024 and 2026. For technical candidates, comments on autonomy and judgment rose the most, while domain expertise shrank as a share of the assessment. In effect, Anthropic is hiring managers of agents.Kent Beck, who created extreme programming, saw the split early. In April 2023 he wrote 90% of My Skills Are Now Worth $0, with a subtitle saying the other 10% were worth 1,000 times more.A portfolio of polished screens shows what a model can now produce, and a record of what you rejected shows judgment.The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 found that seven in 10 employers consider analytical thinking a core skill, the top of its list. For anyone in design, research, or product, that changes what goes in a portfolio and what happens in an interview.Show the decision trail: what the agent proposed, what you cut, and why the result held up with users.In interviews, hand candidates a page of agent output with three planted problems, and watch which ones they catch first.Rebuild Entry-Level RolesThe hardest number in the report concerns people never hired. Junior employees’ share of Anthropic’s technical departments slipped from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and junior technical hires fell from 27% to 9%.Anthropic isn’t alone.This is a warning sign.In Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, Erik Brynjolfsson and two Stanford colleagues found a 13% relative decline in employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in the most exposed occupations. Not every executive agrees.The Register’s AWS CEO says using AI to replace junior staff is ‘Dumbest thing I’ve ever heard’ covered Matt Garman’s argument from August 2025. Juniors cost the least and use the tools the most, he said, and without them nobody will have learned anything in 10 years.The skill to supervise an agent comes from years of doing the work it now does.Lisanne Bainbridge warned of this in Ironies of Automation in 1983: automate most of a job, and people keep its hardest part, the monitoring, without the practice that built their judgment. Entry-level roles in design and research can be rebuilt around review, with a junior making the first call on agent output and a senior explaining every override.That’s an apprenticeship, and it costs less than hiring a senior who never had one.ConclusionIn 1950, the United Auto Workers and General Motors signed a five-year contract that Fortune magazine called the Treaty of Detroit. Walter Reuther’s union gave management room to run the plants, and workers got cost-of-living raises, an annual wage increase, pensions, and health benefits.The report reaches for that same settlement and names Anthropic’s version of it on three points:Broad stock ownershipAn early warning system for jobs at riskA priority on moving people into new roles inside the companyMost of us don’t set compensation policy. We do set what agents show people, when they interrupt, and how review works. Those choices decide whether everyone’s new job as a manager comes with real agency or just a sign-off button.Right now whoever builds the dashboard is making them, and designers, researchers, and product managers should be.The study’s framing is careful. Anthropic is one unusual company, growing fast and building the models it uses, so its practices won’t transfer cleanly to anyone else. The direction is still clear enough to act on this quarter. Output keeps getting cheaper while human attention stays fixed, and the people who decide how it gets spent will shape what these teams become.Action itemsMeasure one workflow. Count the words its agents hand a person in a week, divide by 250, and compare the hours with what anyone has.Tier agent requests. Give every request a severity the agent must justify, batch the routine ones into a daily digest, and keep interruptions for decisions only a person can make.Log decisions publicly. After any meeting that changes direction, post the decision and its owner where agents and colleagues both read.Pair juniors on review. Let a junior make the first call on agent output, with a senior explaining every override.ResourcesWilmers, Catipon, Massenkoff, and McCrory, How employment is changing at Anthropic, Anthropic, 2026Herbert Simon, Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World, 1971University of California, How to sharpen your attention and meet your goals in 2024 (Gloria Mark’s research)The Joint Commission, Sentinel Event Alert 50: Medical device alarm safety in hospitals, 2013Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown, The Coming Age of Calm Technology, Xerox PARC, 1996METR, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, 2025Andrej Karpathy, Andrej Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again), Y Combinator, 2025Patrick Neeman, Automation Bias, UX GuidelinesSimon Willison, Context engineering, 2025 (quoting Tobias Lütke)Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents, 2025Peter Drucker, The Effective Executive, 1967 (quoted from a Fast Company excerpt)Microsoft, The 2025 Annual Work Trend Index: The Frontier Firm is born, 2025Ethan Mollick, Management as AI superpower, One Useful Thing, 2026Christopher Noessel, Designing Agentive Technology, Rosenfeld Media, 2017Kent Beck, 90% of My Skills Are Now Worth $0, 2023World Economic Forum, The Future of Jobs Report 2025, 2025Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine? item.title: What if AI sets us free?
item.description: What can destroy us can also save us. Here’s how I think we can stay in charge of the choice.From the Rocky Horror Picture Show, sourceCasey Harrell is a climate activist. For years, ALS had been slowly taking his speech, until even the people closest to him struggled to understand what he was saying.In July 2023, surgeons at UC Davis implanted tiny sensor arrays in the part of his brain that controls speech. AI learned to read the signals his brain sends when he tries to talk, turned them into words, and spoke those words aloud in a voice rebuilt from old recordings of him.The first time he heard it, he said: “It feels a lot like me.” People who hadn’t heard his voice in a long time cried.I’ve always believed that what can destroy us may also save us. Power can be wielded in many directions. It’s never just black and white.Right now, most people who aren’t tech bros or tech sisses are either avoiding AI altogether or working from a narrow view of what’s actually happening (and what’s possible). Many are scared. The consensus seems to be: AI is coming for us, and that’s probably gonna make everything worse.After a global pandemic and a fresh round of nuclear anxiety, AI feels like the next unprecedented thing. The one that might finally be the nail in humanity’s coffin.But what if it’s not?‘Good’ AI is a choice.What intrigues me about AI is exactly this power: the potential for harm is enormous, which means the potential for good is too. Yin and yang.So what if it all goes right?Humans have always been driven by what if. It’s how we’ve crossed oceans, tamed fire, and ended up, well, here.Exactly here. Collective anxiety, crisis, tech that seems to be racing away from us. It’s no coincidence.But that potential. The opportunity. The blank canvas. The thrill of not knowing exactly what will come out of something is as scary as it is fascinating. And it’s what we’ve always been pushing towards.This exciting sweet spot between what’s possible now and what it might make possible is what got me into designing products for a living.And if that work has taught me one thing, it’s that technology is never neutral. Every product is a stack of decisions: who it serves, what it rewards, what it refuses to do. A feed that keeps you scrolling at 2 am is a design choice. So is a tool that hands you back your evening.And the good AI stories, while harder to find in an endless feed of doom and gloom, are not lucky accidents. In every one of them, someone decided who it was for, put the right people in the room, and kept humans in charge.Good is a choice someone made. What if we make more of those?Yes.What if?What if it cures cancer?AI is already catching cancer earlier.Here in Sweden, Lund University ran the MASAI trial. Around 106,000 women in the Swedish screening programme were split in two: half had their mammograms read the traditional way, half with AI support. The AI group saw 29% more cancers detected. The final results showed 12% fewer cancers slipping through between screenings. Fewer of the aggressive kind, too.As a carrier of the breast cancer gene, with at least one mammogram a year since I turned 30, I’ve spent nights worrying, not about my own risk, but about my daughters’. What if AI solves breast cancer?Zoom out from one disease to all of biology. For 50 years, working out the 3D shape of a single protein could take a scientist years. In 2020, DeepMind’s AlphaFold learned to predict those shapes from a sequence alone. Two years later, its team released predicted structures for more than 200 million proteins. It has since been used by over three million researchers in more than 190 countries. The creators have won the Nobel Prize.And then there are the superbugs. At MIT, researchers trained an AI to scan more than 100 million chemical compounds for ones that could kill bacteria. It found halicin, which killed strains resistant to every known antibiotic in lab tests, and later abaucin. Halicin is named after HAL, the murderous computer in 2001: A Space Odyssey. A reference to its significance.The machine we were taught to fear is finding essential medicine.What if interfaces fit every body and every mind?For all of computing history, people have had to adapt to the machine.AI is starting to flip that. Now.Be My Eyes started in Denmark, founded by a blind furniture craftsman, as an app connecting blind people with sighted volunteers over video. In 2023, it added Be My AI: point your phone at a menu, a medicine label, or your outfit, and get a detailed description back.Casey Harrell, whose story opened this piece, is the far end of the same idea: an interface that adapts so completely it meets you inside your own body — and maybe even mind.So while most AI applications may feel like a boost for mass production, the opposite is also true. For the first time ever, we can create interfaces that shape themselves to us. Our eyes, our voices, our attention spans, our bad days. We can finally kill the norm and build custom at scale.What if it gives artists better access to tools?A friend told me about how low-income filmmakers in his community can now tell their stories due to accessible generative AI for film. And while “made without AI” is more meaningful, showcasing their storytelling skills may be the way to access funding that was limited to privileged groups.I also see this in my life. It’s now easier for me to reformat my writing to make it easier to distribute, type off my handwriting to an online doc, and automate the organization layer of my creative process to allow me more time to actually create.Last month I built an entire app to help me keep track of my ideas as voice notes. It auto-categorizes them and surfaces them back to me based on what I’m doing and where I am. It’s been a game changer for my process and one of the most fun things I’ve done lately: the app’s design is inspired by my kids’ squishy obsession, so the visuals and haptics are satisfying to watch, and tinkering with them was as fun as working on my usual pottery.What if AI gives back to Earth?Rainforest Connection hangs solar-powered listening devices in the canopy. AI listens for chainsaws, trucks and gunshots, and pings rangers’ phones the moment it hears one. The rangers from the Indigenous Tembé community use it to defend their land. The network now covers more than 736,000 hectares in 37 countries. What if we can protect the Earth before it’s too late?Floods affect around 250 million people a year. Google’s Flood Hub uses AI to forecast river floods up to seven days ahead, even where there are no river gauges, and now covers places where 700 million people live, in over 100 countries. Google says flood forecasting in Africa is now on par with Europe. I can imagine there’s even more tech that can do to protect us.There’s more to planet Earth than nature, so…What if it helps unite us, humans?In 2024, DeepMind researchers built an AI mediator, named the Habermas Machine (after one of my favorite German philosophers), and tested it with more than 5,000 people debating divisive issues. People preferred its summaries to a human mediator’s, groups moved closer together, and it worked minority objections into the final conclusion so everyone felt heard. The team behind it trained Habermas to mediate, not to persuade. The job was to find where people already agreed and write it down. If you think about it, it’s the same kind of technology behind the outrage engine of our feeds, just pointed the other way.Could something like this eventually bring us closer together? Make us comfortable discussing and disagreeing again, so we can move toward a compromise and away from extremes and isolation?AI as a peacekeeper. A tempting thought. A machine that helps us hear each other might be a step in the right direction.What if it doesn’t take our jobs?For most, this is the scariest part.And yes, jobs will disappear. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025, based on more than 1,000 employers, expects 92 million jobs to be displaced by 2030 and 170 million new ones created, a net gain of 78 million. The fastest growth is expected in frontline human work like care and education.Forecasts are guesses, though. And even if you believe this optimistic prediction, a net gain is no comfort if the job lost is yours — or if your next one might only be available after years of retraining.I think the truth is somewhere in the middle.In 2024, Klarna announced that its AI assistant was doing the work of 700 customer service agents and handling two-thirds of its customer chats. About a year later, its CEO said the quality had suffered, and the company started hiring humans again.What I’m trying to get at is this:AI built to replace people tends to make things worse. AI built to support people tends to make things better.MASAI didn’t fire radiologists; it gave them back 44% of their reading time. Casey Harrell didn’t need a new voice; he needed his own.Whether AI takes our jobs or transforms them isn’t decided by the technology. It’s decided by people in meeting rooms, choosing what to automate and what to protect. Some of those people are designers. I’m one of them.Most of those people do care.I choose to believe that they, like me, take their responsibility personally and seriously. And that we can and will figure out a way to make AI work for good.What if it actually frees up our time?Last week, my friends over at Sanna, a Norwegian AI-accounting startup, announced that they were introducing a 4-day work week for their accountants.In 2019, Finland’s then-future prime minister asked on a party panel why a four-day week or a six-hour day couldn’t be the next step, and whether eight hours was really the ultimate truth. It never became Finnish policy, but the question stuck. And we now know the answer can be yes. In the UK’s 2022 pilot, 61 companies cut hours with no cut in pay. Revenue held steady, resignations fell by 57%, and 56 of the 61 kept the shorter week.I am hopeful that AI will finally be the technology that doesn’t turn efficiency into more work — because now the gains are so obvious, why would we not spend them on leisure, self-fulfillment, being with each other? Not doing that feels insane to me. I’m sure I’m not the only one.I can imagine it.A Friday that belongs to me: reading, writing, hanging with my kids, or maybe doing nothing at all. The stuff of Renaissance paintings. And maybe our future?From The Laziest People in Art, sourceWhat if it takes us offline?This is my most hopeful what if.Almost every example in this piece still happens on a screen. That’s where we are. Right now. But I don’t think it’s where we’re headed. Screens add a digital layer to life that takes away from our lived experience.I’ve always thought screens were never the point. I’m almost sure you’d agree.We stare at our phones because that’s where the doing happens: the booking, the paying, the replying, the finding. Endless apps, each built to keep us locked in. If AI can do the doing, the reason to stare goes away. You say what you need, and get on with your day. And even further: what if you don’t have to be proactive at all; it can organize based on what it learns about you. The interface becomes secondary. Maybe, it goes away.Think back to Be My AI. A blind user points a phone at a menu, hears what’s on it, and puts the phone back in her pocket. Think of Casey Harrell, speaking with no screen at all. The most advanced interfaces are already the ones that disappear.Wouldn’t it be funny if AI is what finally breaks our phone addictions?And there’s another argument.When content becomes infinite and basically free, it stops being worth much. One-to-infinite, the logic of the feed, gets flooded with sameness. And when everything is generic, what becomes valuable again is the specific: the handmade, the local, the person who actually knows you, the things you can touch. With your heart, mind, and soul.One-to-one, not one-to-infinite (I wrote about this before, here).What if AI pushes our tech obsession so far that it solves it? It runs itself in the background. And we just do us.Humans, human to human, together.Don’t dream it, be it.None of my musings cancel the risks. AI can (and already is) be(ing) used to surveil, manipulate, replace, and harm, and people far more qualified than me are right to sound the alarm.But — I hope this came across in my piece — there is as much potential for good as for evil. Yin and Yang.The future isn’t something that happens to us.It’s something we build. And we can only build toward what we can imagine. If the only story we tell about AI is the one where it ends us, we leave the steering wheel to the people who don’t mind that ending. It’s their greatest weapon: to make us feel defeated, choiceless, numb.From the Rocky Horror Picture show, sourceSo this is for the people who make things.The designers, the writers, the engineers, the product people, the ones in the meeting rooms. We are the ones deciding, one screen, one button, one sentence at a time, what this technology rewards and what it refuses to do.Ask who it’s for.Put the right people in the room.Keep humans in charge. MASAI kept a radiologist in the loop; Rainforest Connection put the tool in the hands of the Tembé rangers rather than a central authority.Let’s build the version you’d want your mother to use at 3 am or your daughter to carry in 20 years.And for everyone else: stay curious. Look past the headlines. Ask for the good version. Demand it. Stray from your feed. Occasionally, turn off the news.Who knows what will happen? What can destroy us may also save us. Believing it might save us is our only chance.So: what if it all goes right?What if, one day, we look at the world we built with it, and say what Casey Harrell said when he heard himself again?It feels a lot like us.Nicole is a Content Designer turned Design Director based in Stockholm, Sweden. She potters, writes poetry, and raises little girls in a house by a meadow. You can follow her writing here or get it directly to your inbox via her publication, eggwoman. Nicole is on LinkedIn. Find her portfolio at nicoletells.com.What if AI sets us free? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
